4.1 Execution control separates graph changes from delivery changes

Across the 120 graph/input pairs in the two-family rewiring study, raw sums match their own explicit reference at every recorded slot and chunk. Recorded floating-point states are not all identical. In E1, population counts also match over all 500 slots, with 84.30% fewer recurrent queue insertions. Active-source edge traversal, graph storage and unit states remain. These are execution checks and queue-traffic measurements, not a claim of graph compression or runtime acceleration. Appendix H retains all E1–E5 comparisons, gain and retention scans, and floating-point state discrepancies.

All five fixtures respecting the grouping conditions preserve every recorded dynamical state bit pattern, stepping decision, chunk status and earliest pending arrival (Table 4). The positive-input, heterogeneous-initial-state and separate-arrival controls produce 20, 22 and 8 spikes, respectively, so their agreement is not limited to silent trajectories. This is observed floating-point equality in the specified fixtures, not an extension of Proposition 1 to arbitrary floating-point executions.

Dropping the zero-amplitude wake-up first changes state and activation at slot 2. Combining equal excitatory and inhibitory contributions into a net zero retains a wake-up at slot 2, but loses both channel states; state differences begin at slot 2 and activation differences at slot 3. Moving inhibitory input from slot 4 to slot 2 changes state at slot 2 even though stepping and chunk status remain matched. All three violating variants retain the same per-unit spike sequences as their references over the 12-slot window. Thus, even spike-sequence agreement can miss internal-state and activation differences in these examples; the tests demonstrate possible failures of grouping outside the stated conditions, not that every condition violation must change spikes.

[[TABLE:4]]

4.2 Matched statistics do not fix identified chunk trajectories

All primary controls exactly preserve the specified per-node degrees and weight multisets. They retain 21.4–23.7% of the original directed adjacency pairs. Although 97.7–98.4% of edge-table rows change target, that row-based measure is not the fraction of original adjacency pairs removed. Table 5 reports the primary homogeneous results; Figure 5 shows every control for both families.

[[TABLE:5]]

[[FIG:5]]

For the homogeneous global burst, population L1 has median 7.21%, whereas identified-chunk L1 has median 28.99%. Whole-window mean rate changes by a median +2.79%, but the post-stimulus 22 ms window changes by +19.33%. Thus a relatively small change in an aggregate readout can coexist with appreciable redistribution across identified chunks and time. The focal-burst chunk difference is larger (median 88.69%), but the inputs also differ in total drive. These results are conditional on the tested graphs and protocols, not evidence that localization alone causes greater sensitivity.

Proposition 2 explains what the preserved statistics constrain for a shared source vector, and Proposition 3 shows why those statistics cannot guarantee universal input reconstruction. Neither predicts the numerical L1 values or makes spike divergence inevitable. The measured closed-loop differences supply the separate empirical evidence. In the heterogeneous controls the population/chunk L1 medians are 11.07%/75.31%, 7.44%/32.54% and 18.33%/98.52% for tonic, global and focal inputs, respectively. Their largest per-arm normalized L1 target-strength change is 16.53%; these are auxiliary sensitivity results, not a pure strength-matched structural comparison.

4.3 Extensive rewiring exceeds the local sensitivity controls

For each of the three inputs, every extensively rewired control has greater 1 ms identified-chunk error than every single-swap control (Table 8; Figure 9). The smallest extensive errors are 45.55%, 23.14% and 73.64% for tonic, global-burst and focal-burst inputs, respectively; the corresponding single-swap maxima are 39.15%, 9.83% and 22.70%. The comparison separates the observed error scales under these controls. It does not establish a causal law relating error to the number of changed edges: the interventions also differ in the sources, paths and endpoint assignments they affect.

[[TABLE:8]]

[[FIG:9]]

Single swaps are not uniformly silent. For each input considered separately, seven of the nineteen controls preserve every raw-slot chunk spike count; their identities differ across inputs. The numbers with zero 1 ms binned error are 10, 7 and 8. The additional zero-bin cases contain two to eight mismatching chunk/slot cells. Thus a zero binned score can conceal timing changes. Shared-original-source input is unchanged within the observation window in four of the 57 swap/input cases, and all four reproduce the ten recorded fields bitwise. However, another 17 cases preserve spikes despite a nonzero shared-source input difference. The input-map diagnostic explains some silent swaps but does not determine nonlinear spike divergence (Figure S6).

All 171 initial-voltage conditions preserve raw-slot chunk spike counts. Their early continuous states differ, but all 125 chunks' ten recorded fields agree with the original at the final slot. This outcome is consistent with the kernel's contraction between equal events, common spike resets and floating-point recoincidence. It is not evidence of general robustness to perturbations at other times or in other state variables. In particular, the separate online pulse experiment in Appendix I.4 can change spike sequences; the initial-voltage control does not contradict that result.

Population aggregation removes a substantial part of the extensive controls' identified-chunk discrepancy: the per-comparison cancellation fraction has medians 83.30%, 75.93% and 82.53% for the three inputs. These are medians of individual ratios, not ratios of the population and chunk medians. Figure S5 shows all defined ratios, and Figure S7 separates cumulative count error from state error over time. The tested small initial changes and single legal swaps do not reach the extensive controls' 1 ms error range. This calibrates the observed magnitudes without identifying an error law per changed edge.

4.4 A fixed swap can change its spike effect across inputs

Among the 19 fixed swap graphs, two preserve every raw-slot chunk spike count under all three inputs, seven differ under all three, and ten switch between equality and difference as the input protocol changes (Figure 10). The intervention itself is fixed within each row: the same endpoints, weights and edit count are used. This paired comparison demonstrates input-dependent visibility of the structural change in the measured spikes. It does not isolate spatial localization, because the protocols also differ in total drive and time course.

The 57 swap/input cases separate into four categories. Four have zero shared-reference-source input discrepancy within the arrival window and reproduce all ten recorded fields bitwise. Seventeen have a nonzero input discrepancy but preserve every raw-slot spike count. Four change raw-slot spikes while preserving all 1 ms bin counts. The remaining 32 change the 1 ms counts. These categories are measured outcomes, not causal stages that every trajectory must pass through (Table 9).

[[TABLE:9]]

[[FIG:10]]

One graph, seed 93006, illustrates all three levels across inputs. Under tonic drive, the shared-source input diagnostic is zero and the recorded states agree. Under global burst, the input diagnostic is nonzero but spikes agree. Under focal burst, 1,268 chunk/slot count cells differ. The paired input contrast thus reaches beyond a change in numerical error magnitude: the same graph modification can be input-invisible, input-visible but spike-invisible, or spike-visible in the tested protocols.

Corollary 1 provides a sufficient explanation for unchanged trajectories when the complete exact-arithmetic hypotheses hold; the source-pair identity makes the role of activity explicit. The empirical diagnostic uses the observed floating-point source sequence and only in-window arrivals. Recorded state equality is checked separately. Conversely, the 17 cases with changed inputs and unchanged spikes show why a nonzero input-map discrepancy is insufficient to predict spike divergence.

4.5 Visibility of fixed swaps under matched inputs

Matching global and focal external drive at every slot leaves 9/19 visibility switches under the original burst and 6/19 under the common rearranged schedule. Preserving each node's amplitude multiset while rearranging time gives 4/19 switches globally and 1/19 under matched focal drive. The matched-focal comparison retains the same binary visibility label for 18/19 swaps. Its one counterexample rules out exact determination by the amplitude multiset, but does not establish frequent switching; unchanged labels do not imply unchanged trajectories. Increasing focal amplitude at fixed support gives 3/19 switches (Table 19; Figure 15, panel A). Each comparison uses the same fixed swap and its own input's original reference. Visibility switching therefore does not require a difference in total drive, and per-node amplitude multisets do not fully determine it. These controls do not quantify how much total drive contributed to the original comparison. Output activity is not matched: original total spike counts for G_B, F_H, G_T and F_HT are 362,200; 280,500; 336,900; and 372,400, respectively.

[[TABLE:19]]

[[FIG:15]]

4.6 Visibility across originals and connection rules

Across the ten legacy graphs, G_B/F_H switches occur in 4–13 of 19 fixed swaps per graph (median 9), despite total-drive equality at every slot. After temporal rearrangement the matched-drive contrast G_T/F_HT gives 6–11 switches. Global temporal rearrangement gives 2–8; matched focal rearrangement gives 0–4. Ring seed 303 has 0/19 focal switches and therefore fails the preset all-graphs switching criterion for that contrast. Seed 99’s 1/19 focal result is a counterexample to exact sufficiency, not evidence of frequent switching. Table 24 and Figure 16 (left) preserve graph-level counts rather than pooling the swaps into an independent sample.

4.7 Heterogeneous LIF replication and saturation of binary visibility

The paired LIF validation contains 600 scientific 300 ms network trajectories: three reused graphs, two neuronal parameter variants, five inputs and 20 graph conditions. In the heterogeneous model, 30 ms G_B/F_H switches are 7/19, 8/19 and 9/19 for seeds 100/201/301. At 300 ms, 116–125 of 125 chunks contain unequal unit spike trains, 401–500 of 500 neurons have fired, and mean rates are 21.59–40.36 Hz. The last 100 ms still contains 1069–1934 spikes. Thus the short-window counterexamples survive genuine within-chunk desynchronization and do not arise from a silent tail. Focal temporal rearrangement remains conditional: seed 201 already has 0/19 switches at 30 ms.

For heterogeneous LIF at 300 ms, every tested swap under every input differs from its own reference. Consequently all five input contrasts have zero visibility switches. This is saturation of the equality label: both sides have become different, not mutually equal. The homogeneous controls still show 2/1/1 G_B/F_H switches across the three graphs. Neither switching nor its disappearance alone describes the error magnitude. Figure 17 (left) shows the complete equality-label composition; the right panel is discussed in Section 4.12.

The complete five-contrast homogeneous/heterogeneous counts are reported in Appendix N. At 30 ms the heterogeneous focal-time contrast is already zero on seed201, while the homogeneous G_B/F_H comparison retains 2/1/1 switches at 300 ms across seeds100/201/301. Thus parameter heterogeneity does not simply increase every input-switch count. Per-unit and chunk-count readouts are both retained; this batch has no case in which unit spikes differ but all chunk slot counts remain equal.

[[FIG:17]]

4.8 Nonzero perturbations can be certified without state equality

Certification first concerns singleton swap cases in the legacy kernel and then separately defined fixed-support weight families; these interventions do not share all structural constraints.

The singleton audit certifies 16 of the 17 previously observed input-changed, spike-equal cases, all four input-equal controls and none of the 36 spike-different cases. The remaining target case, swap93005 under focal input, wakes target 24 at slot 4 rather than reference slot 7. Its unchanged spikes do not satisfy the stronger execution-branch contract. Fourteen of the sixteen certified target cases have affected-target firing; continuous voltage differences may nevertheless reach about 662.84 uncalibrated units. This is spike and branch preservation, not state closeness.

The fixed-support family prototype gives all sixteen target cases nonzero one- and two-parameter certified regions. The fixed five-point and 25-point grids witness respectively five and 25 distinct binary32 weight vectors and event streams in each passing nonzero region; the proof covers the whole region rather than those samples alone. Four target cases per dimension reach the 25% cap, two of which have silent affected targets under focal input. The optimized singleton certificate remains slower than native local replay. In two dimensions the support certificate is cheaper than the implemented rigorous corner envelope, but 25-point replay remains cheaper with its weaker coverage. Appendix J retains the measured costs and failure semantics.

4.9 Regional coverage and actual failures over longer horizons

All 57 original-centred reference conditions match their archived states bitwise. The 912 direction/input conditions require 9,133 radius queries: 652 reach the width tolerance, 98 retain proof gaps and 162 certify to the 25% cap. Every condition has a positive certified lower bound; all 750 finite upper bounds have actual local-replay threshold mismatches. Every lower bound is rechecked. Final-witness prefixes agree bitwise with independent Python replay over 1,787,790 state endpoints; 25 prescribed lower-bound conditions pass 90,000 exact-rational endpoint checks. A separate-process repeat reproduces all nontiming results.

All 1,520 conditions have positive certified lower bounds: 1,049 reach the width tolerance, 230 stop at proof gaps, 239 certify through the 25% cap, and two exhaust the eight refinement steps. No extra refinement is added. All 100 network conditions reproduce 37,500,000 recorded state words exactly in a second run; 40 old network conditions and 608 old radius conditions bridge exactly. Independent Python replay checks 3,169,794 final-witness state endpoints; nine prescribed exact-rational checks cover 5,400 state rows, each with three two-sided coordinate intervals. Appendix K gives stopping and exclusion details. The control protocol was fixed before these new input outcomes; it remains a conditional test on the existing graph, not independent model validation.

Across the ten originals, the tested fixed-support conditions have 14,848 positive lower bounds out of 14,880. The 32 missing positive bounds are zero-radius enclosure failures in two sixteen-direction groups; baseline point replay still agrees. They are not evidence that the unperturbed dynamics fail. The six affinity graphs include 800 silent-target conditions among 8,960 direction/input conditions. Silence and target exclusions are retained, and the original seed-99 16/17 singleton result is not reinterpreted as a multi-graph swap-certification rate. Appendix L gives stage-specific denominators and preserves the failed all-graph focal-time criterion.

Positive certified radii are obtained in 4308/4320 LIF conditions and each covers at least three actually distinct floating weight/event vectors and endpoint state paths. Table 26 retains cap and refinement censoring. The twelve zero lower bounds all occur in heterogeneous seed 301, F_H, target-pair 18, 300 ms; their brackets are [0, 2⁻²⁰], stopped at the preset absolute width tolerance with an actual failure upper witness. Their zero-radius certificates pass. These are resolution-limited lower bounds, not proof that no positive safe interval exists.

[[TABLE:26]]

The median heterogeneous lower radius decreases from 4.19922% at 30 ms to 0.09880% at 300 ms. Lower bounds alone could reflect proof conservatism. The post hoc paired witness test is stronger: U_300<L_30 holds in 710/720 heterogeneous direction conditions and 630/720 homogeneous conditions. Thus a long-prefix failure lies inside a previously certified short-prefix range in those cases. This proves strict range loss for the corresponding executable family, without fitting a decay law, estimating a universal timescale or attributing the loss to chaos. Figure 18 (left) displays every matched bound, including the conditions that do not satisfy the strict test.

[[FIG:18]]

4.10 Equal budget direction order changes across inputs

[[TABLE:14]]

The simplified temporal-margin score orders resolved pairs more consistently than mean activity, time-shifted activity or raw projection magnitude. Resolved coverage is 1,353/2,280, 1,811/2,280 and 1,624/2,280 direction pairs for tonic, global and focal inputs, with 16, 19 and 16 target pairs contributing to the respective macro averages. Unresolved pairs are not counted as correct. Restriction to firing, nonzero-projection conditions leaves the primary averages unchanged. Full sensitivity reaches 1.000 in each input, an algebraic consistency result rather than independent predictive evidence. The primary score locates the failed target and time within one slot in 577/750 witnesses (76.9%); no matched location-frequency baseline has yet been tested.

Across inputs, resolved orders disagree in 371/1,076 jointly resolved direction pairs for tonic/global, 498/1,008 for tonic/focal and 657/1,325 for global/focal (34.5%, 49.4% and 49.6%). At least one reversal occurs in 16, 14 and 14 of the nineteen target pairs, respectively. The near 50% focal comparisons indicate near decorrelation of ordering, not systematic inversion. Input does not merely rescale every direction equally in these comparisons. A lexicographically selected example, rather than the largest effect, is shown in Figure 14.

[[FIG:14]]

Freezing tonic scores yields macro concordance 0.607 under global input and 0.539 under focal input; recomputing the unchanged scoring rule from each input's own reference yields 0.881 and 0.911. This is reference-conditioned ranking, not input-blind transfer. Actual tonic-selected directions show the negative transfer results in Table 15. In particular, relative to mean selection, focal input gives three wins, ten losses, four operational ties and two unresolved comparisons. This supports input-specific direction choice, not a universal superior direction.

[[TABLE:15]]

A post hoc score-only check addresses a two-slot boundary in the original controls. Full-window circular shifts preserve source counts over 300 slots but can change the counts arriving within the observation window; 10, 28 and 8 sources are affected, by at most one chunk firing each. Restricting mean and shift controls to the first 298 source slots preserves delivered counts. Corrected mean concordance is 0.673/0.654/0.725 and corrected shuffle concordance is 0.546/0.467/0.586. The primary ranking advantage and focal transfer failure against mean selection remain. No new perturbation run is added, and these corrected controls do not replace the original locked results.

A post hoc 2×2 factor audit uses the same eligible-slot mask and resolved direction set for every method (Table 18). Joint filtering and margin normalization gives 0.908/0.881/0.911, whereas filtering alone gives 0.587/0.588/0.643 and margin normalization alone 0.527/0.625/0.576. The gain supports complementarity within this score family, not a universal effect of threshold margins alone or a causal mechanism intervention. Mean and shuffled activity are not margin-free controls.

[[TABLE:18]]

Ordering concordance also depends on guaranteed separation. For g in (1,1.1], joint-score macro concordance is 0.735/0.717/0.709; for g > 2 it is 0.970/0.935/0.989. Small g gives only a weak lower bound on separation, not evidence of truly adjacent radii. Unknown orders include both capped and finite-overlap cases. Loose all-comparison score-completion ranges are [0.575, 0.913], [0.699, 0.886] and [0.664, 0.933]; these are not confidence intervals or accuracy estimates and need not be jointly realizable rankings. Appendix K supplies the coverage categories, denominators and excluded targets.

4.11 Direction ordering under controlled inputs and across originals

For weight directions, global/focal matched-drive comparisons disagree in 617/1,237 and 685/1,353 jointly resolved orders (49.88% and 50.63%). Time rearrangement changes 522/1,434 global and 370/1,404 matched-focal orders (36.40% and 26.35%; Figure 15, panel B). These are dependent direction comparisons; near 50% indicates near decorrelation rather than a universal reversal. Spike visibility of endpoint swaps and safety order of fixed-support weight changes remain different interventions.

Using each new input's reference gives joint-score macro concordance 0.906/0.923/0.940 for F_H/G_T/F_HT; frozen G_B scores give 0.480/0.601/0.517 on the same resolved sets. Coverage is 67.06%, 76.32% and 71.67%. Single-factor scores and the matched mean/shuffle controls remain weaker on average (Table 20). For the small guaranteed-separation bin, joint concordance is 0.662/0.726/0.714, so the overall result does not extend to all difficult comparisons. G_B-selected directions also fail to dominate all controls after transfer: against the frozen shuffled choices, F_H and F_HT each yield five wins and eight losses, with six other outcomes. The complete transfer table retains same-direction ties, joint caps and unresolved cases separately in the deposited CSV.

[[TABLE:20]]

Legacy F_H scoring from its own reference yields graph-level macro agreement 0.790–0.939 across the ten graphs, versus 0.471–0.555 for frozen G_B scores (Figure 16, right). The result concerns ordering on resolvable brackets.

4.12 Horizon limits of LIF direction ordering and scores

A direct post hoc comparison of the certified brackets distinguishes order changes from predictor failure. At 300 ms the heterogeneous G_B/F_H comparison resolves both orders for 829 of 1080 possible direction pairs; 394 of those 829 pairs change order. The graph-specific counts are 120/244, 154/327 and 120/258 (Figure 18, right). These are shared-target, shared-direction descriptive counts, not 829 independent replications. They establish concrete changes of direction order under matched total drive, without interpreting a proportion near one half as systematic reversal or as a statistical equivalence to random order.

Input-conditioned F_H joint-score macro agreement is 0.994–1.000 at 30 ms and 0.753–0.826 at 300 ms (Figure 17, right); G_B-frozen scores give 0.567–0.734 and 0.526–0.585, respectively, on the same resolved sets (Table 25). Short-window frozen agreement of 0.734 on seed100 prevents an assertion that all transfer is random. Agreement near one is also conditional on resolved coverage: at 30 ms it is 41.7–76.7%, and two graphs have only two contributing target pairs. These results describe ranking with a known unperturbed reference, not prediction without observing the new input.

The joint score does not uniformly outperform activity controls. For heterogeneous F_H at 300 ms, joint/mean/shuffled agreement is 0.775/0.740/0.676 on seed 100, 0.826/0.774/0.748 on seed 201, and 0.753/0.753/0.759 on seed 301. Close radius pairs are harder: pooling resolved pairs descriptively by the guaranteed separation ratio gives joint agreement 0.676, 0.729 and 0.863 in ratios [1, 1.25), [1.25, 2) and [2, ∞), with 136, 321 and 417 pairs. The primary summaries remain target-pair macro averages. Selecting a direction is a distinct task: frozen G_B joint selection versus random at 300 ms F_H gives 4 wins, 3 losses and 2 unresolved outcomes over nine target pairs, not uniform transfer failure.

Longer windows also expose a scoring implementation boundary. In heterogeneous LIF, at least one eligible reference margin falls below the fixed 2⁻²⁰ V floor in 15/45 target-pair/input groups at 30 ms, 34/45 at 100 ms and 45/45 at 300 ms. These group counts mean at least one clipped eligible time in each counted group; they do not measure the fraction of clipped times or show that clipping dominates the score. This post hoc diagnostic was not used to retune the score. It prevents attributing all ranking degradation to a physiological mechanism or claiming that the full frozen-branch score must order radii exactly. The certifier uses the actual thresholds, not that scoring floor.

[[TABLE:25]]

4.13 Local and extensive changes have different temporal error composition

The following temporal-error, dose and selection results concern the seed99 legacy kernel and serve as interpretive controls for the two research questions; they are not new LIF tests.

For the 12 single-swap cases per input with nonzero raw-slot error, the median fractions D_count/D_slot are 4.34%, 5.93% and 12.66% for tonic, global-burst and focal-burst inputs. Across all 19 extensive controls per input, the corresponding medians are 56.77%, 58.36% and 52.55% (Figure 11). Thus, in each input, most of the typical single-swap discrepancy cancels during time accumulation within the same identified node, whereas more than half of the extensive discrepancy remains in identified-node cumulative counts. The difference in these measured fractions is not imposed by the triangle inequality, which only bounds each fraction between zero and one (Table 10).

[[TABLE:10]]

The temporal-first decomposition also distinguishes cancellation within nodes from the subsequent cancellation between nodes. It identifies what the readout removes, not the dynamical mechanism that generated the discrepancies. In particular, time cancellation can pair excesses and deficits separated by much of the window; it does not establish small temporal jitter or one-to-one displaced spikes. A lower cumulative-count discrepancy does not imply a close fine trajectory. The comparison is conditional on spike-different cases; the seven spike-identical swaps under each input have undefined composition fractions and remain reported separately.

These are different intervention ensembles. Extensive controls remove 76.3–78.6% of original adjacency pairs, compared with 0.07030% for a single swap, approximately 1,100 times less. Their discrepancy composition therefore does not identify an effect of scale independent of endpoint selection, nor a universal relation between edit budget and error composition.

[[FIG:11]]

A paired post hoc comparison of ten complete random chains supplies intermediate edit budgets without linking unrelated interventions (Table 17). At 0.984%, 1.968% and 9.912% adjacency edits, mean normalized raw-slot discrepancy X is 1.0659, 1.0746 and 1.1463; mean cumulative-count discrepancy Y is 0.2783, 0.2884 and 0.4380. Mean retained fractions are 25.47%, 26.60% and 38.33%. All thirty trajectories have nonzero slot and count error. The lowest tested budget already gives a large slot discrepancy; increasing the budget mainly enlarges cumulative-count discrepancy relative to the modest change in mean slot discrepancy. Normalized L1 is not a correlation coefficient, and one is not a decorrelation or saturation threshold.

[[TABLE:17]]

From the lowest to highest budget, mean Y rises 15.97 percentage points. The exact per-chain product decomposition assigns 2.29 points to the magnitude term and 13.68 to the retained-fraction term. This is not a causal attribution. From 1% to 2%, X decreases in seven chains and increases in three, while Y increases in five and decreases in five. Across all three budgets, X, Y and R are nonmonotonic in seven, six and five chains, respectively. Even at 9.912%, the mean fraction canceled within nodes is 61.67%; cumulative-count bias does not dominate by default. The budgets have overlapping composition ranges and do not support a universal monotonic dose law. Appendix K retains paired changes and all bin-offset readouts.

4.14 Readout robustness preserves the identified-node range separation

At the raw 0.1 ms resolution, median single-swap count errors are 0.50%, 9.69% and 40.38%; with the original 1 ms bins, they are 0%, 1.35% and 7.05%. The largest focal-burst single-swap raw-slot error is 98.58%. Minimal edits therefore need not produce a small fine-time trajectory error, even when binning substantially lowers the score.

For every common width and offset in the five-width scan, the smallest extensive identified-chunk error exceeds the largest single-swap error: 1,089 of 1,089 input/width/offset readouts (Figure 12). At 1 ms, the smallest gaps over the ten common offsets are 6.40, 13.14 and 50.00 percentage points for the three inputs. This is an exhaustive check over the specified offsets of the existing trajectories, not 1,089 independent confirmations or evidence for untested inputs. E/I-pooled and globally pooled ranges overlap in most settings; the uniform separation applies to the identified-node readout.

[[FIG:12]]

The bin-free exponential-filter score also preserves strict range separation in all 15 input/time-constant combinations. This makes the observed ordering more than an artifact of the original 1 ms bin origin. It does not make error magnitudes readout-independent, guarantee the ordering under all possible spike distances, or show that temporal cancellation consists of short displacements. The robustness claim concerns the separation of the two sampled intervention ensembles while node identity is retained.

4.15 Activity scores and closed loop fidelity at fixed edit budgets

At 9.9121% adjacency replacement, minimizing the coactivity score lowers it relative to the random choice in all ten banks. The paired relative reductions have mean 19.33%, median 19.82% and range 6.00–30.35%. This improvement follows selection from the shared candidate bank; it does not establish a dynamical benefit. Mean primary held-out raw-slot L1 is 1.1161 for random selection and 1.2440 for coactivity selection. The paired difference is +0.1279, or +12.79 percentage points, with eight losses and two wins for coactivity. The corresponding differences against mean-activity and shuffled selection are +0.0324 and +0.0112. Training-input raw-slot error also increases by 0.09255 on average, with eight losses and two wins, so the mismatch is already present under the input used to compute the scores.

The predefined secondary readouts vary with the input. For the split-burst condition on the original target mask, coactivity-minus-random mean differences are −6.23 percentage points for 1 ms L1, −6.68 points for cumulative-count L1, −0.4380 for the normalized squared exponential-filter distance and −0.0776 for standardized state RMS. All four improve in the same seven banks, while raw-slot L1 worsens in eight. Their correlated improvements do not replace the primary outcome. The interpretation of this readout-dependent reversal was formed after the results were observed.

At 0.9842% and 1.9684% edits, paired relative reductions of the coactivity score against random have means 54.87% and 46.90%, respectively, with nine strict reductions and one shared choice at each budget. Training raw-slot L1 improves by mean differences −0.08591 and −0.11382, or −8.59 and −11.38 percentage points; each budget has seven wins, one tie and two losses. Mean coactivity errors are nevertheless 0.9799 and 0.9608, so these are relative improvements at substantial absolute discrepancy (Table 11; Figure 13).

[[TABLE:11]]

The 0.9842% budget has mean paired differences +0.04133 against mean-activity selection and +0.004404 against shuffled selection. It fails the comparator safeguards. The 1.9684% budget passes its individual rule, but the protocol requires both budgets to pass. The joint decision is therefore to stop, and no lower-budget changed-input condition is simulated. Coactivity and shuffled selection choose the same graph in nine of ten banks at each budget; their remaining mean differences are driven by one bank per budget. These comparisons do not isolate a benefit specific to cross-source coactivity. Table 12 reports the paired comparisons against random, mean-activity and shuffled selection, together with the stopping criteria.

[[TABLE:12]]

None of the 1,280 lower-budget candidates has a zero value for any of the four recorded scores, including the analytic shuffle diagnostic. Across the 80 selector–budget training records, none has zero raw-slot, 1 ms or cumulative-count discrepancy, or exact agreement of all ten recorded fields. The records correspond to 57 unique selected graphs plus one original reference, giving 58 scientific runs and one separate technical repetition. Thus the observed selection gains are not a collection of exact-preservation cases hidden by averaging, and lower-budget transfer remains untested. The three budgets, nested candidate construction and re-selection at each budget do not establish a critical edit fraction or a monotonic error law.

4.3 Extensive rewiring exceeds the local sensitivity controls

For each of the three inputs, every extensively rewired control has greater 1 ms identified-chunk error than every single-swap control (Table 8; Figure 9). The smallest extensive errors are 45.55%, 23.14% and 73.64% for tonic, global-burst and focal-burst inputs, respectively; the corresponding single-swap maxima are 39.15%, 9.83% and 22.70%. The comparison separates the observed error scales under these controls. It does not establish a causal law relating error to the number of changed edges: the interventions also differ in the sources, paths and endpoint assignments they affect.

[[TABLE:8]]

[[FIG:9]]

Single swaps are not uniformly silent. For each input considered separately, seven of the nineteen controls preserve every raw-slot chunk spike count; their identities differ across inputs. The numbers with zero 1 ms binned error are 10, 7 and 8. The additional zero-bin cases contain two to eight mismatching chunk/slot cells. Thus a zero binned score can conceal timing changes. Shared-original-source input is unchanged within the observation window in four of the 57 swap/input cases, and all four reproduce the ten recorded fields bitwise. However, another 17 cases preserve spikes despite a nonzero shared-source input difference. The input-map diagnostic explains some silent swaps but does not determine nonlinear spike divergence (Figure S6).

All 171 initial-voltage conditions preserve raw-slot chunk spike counts. Their early continuous states differ, but all 125 chunks' ten recorded fields agree with the original at the final slot. This outcome is consistent with the kernel's contraction between equal events, common spike resets and floating-point recoincidence. It is not evidence of general robustness to perturbations at other times or in other state variables. In particular, the separate online pulse experiment in Appendix I.4 can change spike sequences; the initial-voltage control does not contradict that result.

Population aggregation removes a substantial part of the extensive controls' identified-chunk discrepancy: the per-comparison cancellation fraction has medians 83.30%, 75.93% and 82.53% for the three inputs. These are medians of individual ratios, not ratios of the population and chunk medians. Figure S5 shows all defined ratios, and Figure S7 separates cumulative count error from state error over time. The tested small initial changes and single legal swaps do not reach the extensive controls' 1 ms error range. This calibrates the observed magnitudes without identifying an error law per changed edge.

4.4 A fixed swap can change its spike effect across inputs

Among the 19 fixed swap graphs, two preserve every raw-slot chunk spike count under all three inputs, seven differ under all three, and ten switch between equality and difference as the input protocol changes (Figure 10). The intervention itself is fixed within each row: the same endpoints, weights and edit count are used. This paired comparison demonstrates input-dependent visibility of the structural change in the measured spikes. It does not isolate spatial localization, because the protocols also differ in total drive and time course.

The 57 swap/input cases separate into four categories. Four have zero shared-reference-source input discrepancy within the arrival window and reproduce all ten recorded fields bitwise. Seventeen have a nonzero input discrepancy but preserve every raw-slot spike count. Four change raw-slot spikes while preserving all 1 ms bin counts. The remaining 32 change the 1 ms counts. These categories are measured outcomes, not causal stages that every trajectory must pass through (Table 9).

[[TABLE:9]]

[[FIG:10]]

One graph, seed 93006, illustrates all three levels across inputs. Under tonic drive, the shared-source input diagnostic is zero and the recorded states agree. Under global burst, the input diagnostic is nonzero but spikes agree. Under focal burst, 1,268 chunk/slot count cells differ. The paired input contrast thus reaches beyond a change in numerical error magnitude: the same graph modification can be input-invisible, input-visible but spike-invisible, or spike-visible in the tested protocols.

Corollary 1 provides a sufficient explanation for unchanged trajectories when the complete exact-arithmetic hypotheses hold; the source-pair identity makes the role of activity explicit. The empirical diagnostic uses the observed floating-point source sequence and only in-window arrivals. Recorded state equality is checked separately. Conversely, the 17 cases with changed inputs and unchanged spikes show why a nonzero input-map discrepancy is insufficient to predict spike divergence.

4.5 Visibility of fixed swaps under matched inputs

Matching global and focal external drive at every slot leaves 9/19 visibility switches under the original burst and 6/19 under the common rearranged schedule. Preserving each node's amplitude multiset while rearranging time gives 4/19 switches globally and 1/19 under matched focal drive. The matched-focal comparison retains the same binary visibility label for 18/19 swaps. Its one counterexample rules out exact determination by the amplitude multiset, but does not establish frequent switching; unchanged labels do not imply unchanged trajectories. Increasing focal amplitude at fixed support gives 3/19 switches (Table 19; Figure 15, panel A). Each comparison uses the same fixed swap and its own input's original reference. Visibility switching therefore does not require a difference in total drive, and per-node amplitude multisets do not fully determine it. These controls do not quantify how much total drive contributed to the original comparison. Output activity is not matched: original total spike counts for G_B, F_H, G_T and F_HT are 362,200; 280,500; 336,900; and 372,400, respectively.

[[TABLE:19]]

[[FIG:15]]

4.6 Visibility across originals and connection rules

Across the ten legacy graphs, G_B/F_H switches occur in 4–13 of 19 fixed swaps per graph (median 9), despite total-drive equality at every slot. After temporal rearrangement the matched-drive contrast G_T/F_HT gives 6–11 switches. Global temporal rearrangement gives 2–8; matched focal rearrangement gives 0–4. Ring seed 303 has 0/19 focal switches and therefore fails the preset all-graphs switching criterion for that contrast. Seed 99’s 1/19 focal result is a counterexample to exact sufficiency, not evidence of frequent switching. Table 24 and Figure 16 (left) preserve graph-level counts rather than pooling the swaps into an independent sample.

4.7 Heterogeneous LIF replication and saturation of binary visibility

The paired LIF validation contains 600 scientific 300 ms network trajectories: three reused graphs, two neuronal parameter variants, five inputs and 20 graph conditions. In the heterogeneous model, 30 ms G_B/F_H switches are 7/19, 8/19 and 9/19 for seeds 100/201/301. At 300 ms, 116–125 of 125 chunks contain unequal unit spike trains, 401–500 of 500 neurons have fired, and mean rates are 21.59–40.36 Hz. The last 100 ms still contains 1069–1934 spikes. Thus the short-window counterexamples survive genuine within-chunk desynchronization and do not arise from a silent tail. Focal temporal rearrangement remains conditional: seed 201 already has 0/19 switches at 30 ms.

For heterogeneous LIF at 300 ms, every tested swap under every input differs from its own reference. Consequently all five input contrasts have zero visibility switches. This is saturation of the equality label: both sides have become different, not mutually equal. The homogeneous controls still show 2/1/1 G_B/F_H switches across the three graphs. Neither switching nor its disappearance alone describes the error magnitude. Figure 17 (left) shows the complete equality-label composition; the right panel is discussed in Section 4.12.

The complete five-contrast homogeneous/heterogeneous counts are reported in Appendix N. At 30 ms the heterogeneous focal-time contrast is already zero on seed201, while the homogeneous G_B/F_H comparison retains 2/1/1 switches at 300 ms across seeds100/201/301. Thus parameter heterogeneity does not simply increase every input-switch count. Per-unit and chunk-count readouts are both retained; this batch has no case in which unit spikes differ but all chunk slot counts remain equal.

[[FIG:17]]

4.8 Nonzero perturbations can be certified without state equality

Certification first concerns singleton swap cases in the legacy kernel and then separately defined fixed-support weight families; these interventions do not share all structural constraints.

The singleton audit certifies 16 of the 17 previously observed input-changed, spike-equal cases, all four input-equal controls and none of the 36 spike-different cases. The remaining target case, swap93005 under focal input, wakes target 24 at slot 4 rather than reference slot 7. Its unchanged spikes do not satisfy the stronger execution-branch contract. Fourteen of the sixteen certified target cases have affected-target firing; continuous voltage differences may nevertheless reach about 662.84 uncalibrated units. This is spike and branch preservation, not state closeness.

The fixed-support family prototype gives all sixteen target cases nonzero one- and two-parameter certified regions. The fixed five-point and 25-point grids witness respectively five and 25 distinct binary32 weight vectors and event streams in each passing nonzero region; the proof covers the whole region rather than those samples alone. Four target cases per dimension reach the 25% cap, two of which have silent affected targets under focal input. The optimized singleton certificate remains slower than native local replay. In two dimensions the support certificate is cheaper than the implemented rigorous corner envelope, but 25-point replay remains cheaper with its weaker coverage. Appendix J retains the measured costs and failure semantics.

4.9 Regional coverage and actual failures over longer horizons

All 57 original-centred reference conditions match their archived states bitwise. The 912 direction/input conditions require 9,133 radius queries: 652 reach the width tolerance, 98 retain proof gaps and 162 certify to the 25% cap. Every condition has a positive certified lower bound; all 750 finite upper bounds have actual local-replay threshold mismatches. Every lower bound is rechecked. Final-witness prefixes agree bitwise with independent Python replay over 1,787,790 state endpoints; 25 prescribed lower-bound conditions pass 90,000 exact-rational endpoint checks. A separate-process repeat reproduces all nontiming results.

All 1,520 conditions have positive certified lower bounds: 1,049 reach the width tolerance, 230 stop at proof gaps, 239 certify through the 25% cap, and two exhaust the eight refinement steps. No extra refinement is added. All 100 network conditions reproduce 37,500,000 recorded state words exactly in a second run; 40 old network conditions and 608 old radius conditions bridge exactly. Independent Python replay checks 3,169,794 final-witness state endpoints; nine prescribed exact-rational checks cover 5,400 state rows, each with three two-sided coordinate intervals. Appendix K gives stopping and exclusion details. The control protocol was fixed before these new input outcomes; it remains a conditional test on the existing graph, not independent model validation.

Across the ten originals, the tested fixed-support conditions have 14,848 positive lower bounds out of 14,880. The 32 missing positive bounds are zero-radius enclosure failures in two sixteen-direction groups; baseline point replay still agrees. They are not evidence that the unperturbed dynamics fail. The six affinity graphs include 800 silent-target conditions among 8,960 direction/input conditions. Silence and target exclusions are retained, and the original seed-99 16/17 singleton result is not reinterpreted as a multi-graph swap-certification rate. Appendix L gives stage-specific denominators and preserves the failed all-graph focal-time criterion.

Positive certified radii are obtained in 4308/4320 LIF conditions and each covers at least three actually distinct floating weight/event vectors and endpoint state paths. Table 26 retains cap and refinement censoring. The twelve zero lower bounds all occur in heterogeneous seed 301, F_H, target-pair 18, 300 ms; their brackets are [0, 2⁻²⁰], stopped at the preset absolute width tolerance with an actual failure upper witness. Their zero-radius certificates pass. These are resolution-limited lower bounds, not proof that no positive safe interval exists.

[[TABLE:26]]

The median heterogeneous lower radius decreases from 4.19922% at 30 ms to 0.09880% at 300 ms. Lower bounds alone could reflect proof conservatism. The post hoc paired witness test is stronger: U_300<L_30 holds in 710/720 heterogeneous direction conditions and 630/720 homogeneous conditions. Thus a long-prefix failure lies inside a previously certified short-prefix range in those cases. This proves strict range loss for the corresponding executable family, without fitting a decay law, estimating a universal timescale or attributing the loss to chaos. Figure 18 (left) displays every matched bound, including the conditions that do not satisfy the strict test.

4.10 Equal budget direction order changes across inputs

Table 14 reports macro ordering concordance on the resolved radius pairs.

[[TABLE:14]]

The simplified temporal-margin score orders resolved pairs more consistently than mean activity, time-shifted activity or raw projection magnitude. Resolved coverage is 1,353/2,280, 1,811/2,280 and 1,624/2,280 direction pairs for tonic, global and focal inputs, with 16, 19 and 16 target pairs contributing to the respective macro averages. Unresolved pairs are not counted as correct. Restriction to firing, nonzero-projection conditions leaves the primary averages unchanged. Full sensitivity reaches 1.000 in each input, an algebraic consistency result rather than independent predictive evidence. The primary score locates the failed target and time within one slot in 577/750 witnesses (76.9%); no matched location-frequency baseline has yet been tested.

Across inputs, resolved orders disagree in 371/1,076 jointly resolved direction pairs for tonic/global, 498/1,008 for tonic/focal and 657/1,325 for global/focal (34.5%, 49.4% and 49.6%). At least one reversal occurs in 16, 14 and 14 of the nineteen target pairs, respectively. The near 50% focal comparisons indicate near decorrelation of ordering, not systematic inversion. Input does not merely rescale every direction equally in these comparisons. A lexicographically selected example, rather than the largest effect, is shown in Figure 14.

[[FIG:14]]

Freezing tonic scores yields macro concordance 0.607 under global input and 0.539 under focal input; recomputing the unchanged scoring rule from each input's own reference yields 0.881 and 0.911. This is reference-conditioned ranking, not input-blind transfer. Actual tonic-selected directions show the negative transfer results in Table 15. In particular, relative to mean selection, focal input gives three wins, ten losses, four operational ties and two unresolved comparisons. This supports input-specific direction choice, not a universal superior direction.

[[TABLE:15]]

A post hoc score-only check addresses a two-slot boundary in the original controls. Full-window circular shifts preserve source counts over 300 slots but can change the counts arriving within the observation window; 10, 28 and 8 sources are affected, by at most one chunk firing each. Restricting mean and shift controls to the first 298 source slots preserves delivered counts. Corrected mean concordance is 0.673/0.654/0.725 and corrected shuffle concordance is 0.546/0.467/0.586. The primary ranking advantage and focal transfer failure against mean selection remain. No new perturbation run is added, and these corrected controls do not replace the original locked results.

A post hoc 2×2 factor audit uses the same eligible-slot mask and resolved direction set for every method (Table 18). Joint filtering and margin normalization gives 0.908/0.881/0.911, whereas filtering alone gives 0.587/0.588/0.643 and margin normalization alone 0.527/0.625/0.576. The gain supports complementarity within this score family, not a universal effect of threshold margins alone or a causal mechanism intervention. Mean and shuffled activity are not margin-free controls.

[[TABLE:18]]

Ordering concordance also depends on guaranteed separation. For g in (1,1.1], joint-score macro concordance is 0.735/0.717/0.709; for g > 2 it is 0.970/0.935/0.989. Small g gives only a weak lower bound on separation, not evidence of truly adjacent radii. Unknown orders include both capped and finite-overlap cases. Loose all-comparison score-completion ranges are [0.575, 0.913], [0.699, 0.886] and [0.664, 0.933]; these are not confidence intervals or accuracy estimates and need not be jointly realizable rankings. Appendix K supplies the coverage categories, denominators and excluded targets.

4.11 Direction ordering under controlled inputs and across originals

For weight directions, global/focal matched-drive comparisons disagree in 617/1,237 and 685/1,353 jointly resolved orders (49.88% and 50.63%). Time rearrangement changes 522/1,434 global and 370/1,404 matched-focal orders (36.40% and 26.35%; Figure 15, panel B). These are dependent direction comparisons; near 50% indicates near decorrelation rather than a universal reversal. Spike visibility of endpoint swaps and safety order of fixed-support weight changes remain different interventions.

Using each new input's reference gives joint-score macro concordance 0.906/0.923/0.940 for F_H/G_T/F_HT; frozen G_B scores give 0.480/0.601/0.517 on the same resolved sets. Coverage is 67.06%, 76.32% and 71.67%. Single-factor scores and the matched mean/shuffle controls remain weaker on average (Table 20). For the small guaranteed-separation bin, joint concordance is 0.662/0.726/0.714, so the overall result does not extend to all difficult comparisons. G_B-selected directions also fail to dominate all controls after transfer: against the frozen shuffled choices, F_H and F_HT each yield five wins and eight losses, with six other outcomes. The complete transfer table retains same-direction ties, joint caps and unresolved cases separately in the deposited CSV.

[[TABLE:20]]

Legacy F_H scoring from its own reference yields graph-level macro agreement 0.790–0.939 across the ten graphs, versus 0.471–0.555 for frozen G_B scores (Figure 16, right). The result concerns ordering on resolvable brackets.

4.12 Horizon limits of LIF direction ordering and scores

A direct post hoc comparison of the certified brackets distinguishes order changes from predictor failure. At 300 ms the heterogeneous G_B/F_H comparison resolves both orders for 829 of 1080 possible direction pairs; 394 of those 829 pairs change order. The graph-specific counts are 120/244, 154/327 and 120/258 (Figure 18, right). These are shared-target, shared-direction descriptive counts, not 829 independent replications. They establish concrete changes of direction order under matched total drive, without interpreting a proportion near one half as systematic reversal or as a statistical equivalence to random order.

Input-conditioned F_H joint-score macro agreement is 0.994–1.000 at 30 ms and 0.753–0.826 at 300 ms (Figure 17, right); G_B-frozen scores give 0.567–0.734 and 0.526–0.585, respectively, on the same resolved sets (Table 25). Short-window frozen agreement of 0.734 on seed100 prevents an assertion that all transfer is random. Agreement near one is also conditional on resolved coverage: at 30 ms it is 41.7–76.7%, and two graphs have only two contributing target pairs. These results describe ranking with a known unperturbed reference, not prediction without observing the new input.

The joint score does not uniformly outperform activity controls. For heterogeneous F_H at 300 ms, joint/mean/shuffled agreement is 0.775/0.740/0.676 on seed 100, 0.826/0.774/0.748 on seed 201, and 0.753/0.753/0.759 on seed 301. Close radius pairs are harder: pooling resolved pairs descriptively by the guaranteed separation ratio gives joint agreement 0.676, 0.729 and 0.863 in ratios [1, 1.25), [1.25, 2) and [2, ∞), with 136, 321 and 417 pairs. The primary summaries remain target-pair macro averages. Selecting a direction is a distinct task: frozen G_B joint selection versus random at 300 ms F_H gives 4 wins, 3 losses and 2 unresolved outcomes over nine target pairs, not uniform transfer failure.

Longer windows also expose a scoring implementation boundary. In heterogeneous LIF, at least one eligible reference margin falls below the fixed 2⁻²⁰ V floor in 15/45 target-pair/input groups at 30 ms, 34/45 at 100 ms and 45/45 at 300 ms. These group counts mean at least one clipped eligible time in each counted group; they do not measure the fraction of clipped times or show that clipping dominates the score. This post hoc diagnostic was not used to retune the score. It prevents attributing all ranking degradation to a physiological mechanism or claiming that the full frozen-branch score must order radii exactly. The certifier uses the actual thresholds, not that scoring floor.

[[TABLE:25]]

4.13 Local and extensive changes have different temporal error composition

The following temporal-error, dose and selection results concern the seed99 legacy kernel and serve as interpretive controls for the two research questions; they are not new LIF tests.

For the 12 single-swap cases per input with nonzero raw-slot error, the median fractions D_count/D_slot are 4.34%, 5.93% and 12.66% for tonic, global-burst and focal-burst inputs. Across all 19 extensive controls per input, the corresponding medians are 56.77%, 58.36% and 52.55% (Figure 11). Thus, in each input, most of the typical single-swap discrepancy cancels during time accumulation within the same identified node, whereas more than half of the extensive discrepancy remains in identified-node cumulative counts. The difference in these measured fractions is not imposed by the triangle inequality, which only bounds each fraction between zero and one (Table 10).

[[TABLE:10]]

The temporal-first decomposition also distinguishes cancellation within nodes from the subsequent cancellation between nodes. It identifies what the readout removes, not the dynamical mechanism that generated the discrepancies. In particular, time cancellation can pair excesses and deficits separated by much of the window; it does not establish small temporal jitter or one-to-one displaced spikes. A lower cumulative-count discrepancy does not imply a close fine trajectory. The comparison is conditional on spike-different cases; the seven spike-identical swaps under each input have undefined composition fractions and remain reported separately.

These are different intervention ensembles. Extensive controls remove 76.3–78.6% of original adjacency pairs, compared with 0.07030% for a single swap, approximately 1,100 times less. Their discrepancy composition therefore does not identify an effect of scale independent of endpoint selection, nor a universal relation between edit budget and error composition.

[[FIG:11]]

A paired post hoc comparison of ten complete random chains supplies intermediate edit budgets without linking unrelated interventions (Table 17). At 0.984%, 1.968% and 9.912% adjacency edits, mean normalized raw-slot discrepancy X is 1.0659, 1.0746 and 1.1463; mean cumulative-count discrepancy Y is 0.2783, 0.2884 and 0.4380. Mean retained fractions are 25.47%, 26.60% and 38.33%. All thirty trajectories have nonzero slot and count error. The lowest tested budget already gives a large slot discrepancy; increasing the budget mainly enlarges cumulative-count discrepancy relative to the modest change in mean slot discrepancy. Normalized L1 is not a correlation coefficient, and one is not a decorrelation or saturation threshold.

[[TABLE:17]]

From the lowest to highest budget, mean Y rises 15.97 percentage points. The exact per-chain product decomposition assigns 2.29 points to the magnitude term and 13.68 to the retained-fraction term. This is not a causal attribution. From 1% to 2%, X decreases in seven chains and increases in three, while Y increases in five and decreases in five. Across all three budgets, X, Y and R are nonmonotonic in seven, six and five chains, respectively. Even at 9.912%, the mean fraction canceled within nodes is 61.67%; cumulative-count bias does not dominate by default. The budgets have overlapping composition ranges and do not support a universal monotonic dose law. Appendix K retains paired changes and all bin-offset readouts.

4.14 Readout robustness preserves the identified-node range separation

At the raw 0.1 ms resolution, median single-swap count errors are 0.50%, 9.69% and 40.38%; with the original 1 ms bins, they are 0%, 1.35% and 7.05%. The largest focal-burst single-swap raw-slot error is 98.58%. Minimal edits therefore need not produce a small fine-time trajectory error, even when binning substantially lowers the score.

For every common width and offset in the five-width scan, the smallest extensive identified-chunk error exceeds the largest single-swap error: 1,089 of 1,089 input/width/offset readouts (Figure 12). At 1 ms, the smallest gaps over the ten common offsets are 6.40, 13.14 and 50.00 percentage points for the three inputs. This is an exhaustive check over the specified offsets of the existing trajectories, not 1,089 independent confirmations or evidence for untested inputs. E/I-pooled and globally pooled ranges overlap in most settings; the uniform separation applies to the identified-node readout.

[[FIG:12]]

The bin-free exponential-filter score also preserves strict range separation in all 15 input/time-constant combinations. This makes the observed ordering more than an artifact of the original 1 ms bin origin. It does not make error magnitudes readout-independent, guarantee the ordering under all possible spike distances, or show that temporal cancellation consists of short displacements. The robustness claim concerns the separation of the two sampled intervention ensembles while node identity is retained.

4.15 Activity scores and closed loop fidelity at fixed edit budgets

At 9.9121% adjacency replacement, minimizing the coactivity score lowers it relative to the random choice in all ten banks. The paired relative reductions have mean 19.33%, median 19.82% and range 6.00–30.35%. This improvement follows selection from the shared candidate bank; it does not establish a dynamical benefit. Mean primary held-out raw-slot L1 is 1.1161 for random selection and 1.2440 for coactivity selection. The paired difference is +0.1279, or +12.79 percentage points, with eight losses and two wins for coactivity. The corresponding differences against mean-activity and shuffled selection are +0.0324 and +0.0112. Training-input raw-slot error also increases by 0.09255 on average, with eight losses and two wins, so the mismatch is already present under the input used to compute the scores.

The predefined secondary readouts vary with the input. For the split-burst condition on the original target mask, coactivity-minus-random mean differences are −6.23 percentage points for 1 ms L1, −6.68 points for cumulative-count L1, −0.4380 for the normalized squared exponential-filter distance and −0.0776 for standardized state RMS. All four improve in the same seven banks, while raw-slot L1 worsens in eight. Their correlated improvements do not replace the primary outcome. The interpretation of this readout-dependent reversal was formed after the results were observed.

At 0.9842% and 1.9684% edits, paired relative reductions of the coactivity score against random have means 54.87% and 46.90%, respectively, with nine strict reductions and one shared choice at each budget. Training raw-slot L1 improves by mean differences −0.08591 and −0.11382, or −8.59 and −11.38 percentage points; each budget has seven wins, one tie and two losses. Mean coactivity errors are nevertheless 0.9799 and 0.9608, so these are relative improvements at substantial absolute discrepancy (Table 11; Figure 13).

[[TABLE:11]]

The 0.9842% budget has mean paired differences +0.04133 against mean-activity selection and +0.004404 against shuffled selection. It fails the comparator safeguards. The 1.9684% budget passes its individual rule, but the protocol requires both budgets to pass. The joint decision is therefore to stop, and no lower-budget changed-input condition is simulated. Coactivity and shuffled selection choose the same graph in nine of ten banks at each budget; their remaining mean differences are driven by one bank per budget. These comparisons do not isolate a benefit specific to cross-source coactivity. Table 12 reports the paired comparisons against random, mean-activity and shuffled selection, together with the stopping criteria.

[[TABLE:12]]

None of the 1,280 lower-budget candidates has a zero value for any of the four recorded scores, including the analytic shuffle diagnostic. Across the 80 selector–budget training records, none has zero raw-slot, 1 ms or cumulative-count discrepancy, or exact agreement of all ten recorded fields. The records correspond to 57 unique selected graphs plus one original reference, giving 58 scientific runs and one separate technical repetition. Thus the observed selection gains are not a collection of exact-preservation cases hidden by averaging, and lower-budget transfer remains untested. The three budgets, nested candidate construction and re-selection at each budget do not establish a critical edit fraction or a monotonic error law.

J.1 Sufficient condition and proof

Proposition 4 (common branch finite horizon enclosure). Fix a deterministic discrete implementation, initial state, external input and finite window. 4.1 执行对照区分图变化与投递变化

在两个图族的120个图／输入组合中，原始求和在每个记录时间槽和块上均与其自身显式参考一致，但所记录浮点状态并非全部相同。E1的500个时间槽中群体计数也完全匹配，递归队列插入减少84.30%。活跃源边遍历、图存储及单元状态仍保留。这些是执行检查与队列流量测量，不是图压缩或运行时间加速的证据。附录H保留全部E1–E5比较、增益和保留率扫描，以及浮点状态差异。

五个满足分组条件的测试，其全部记录动力学状态的位模式、步进决策、块状态和最早待处理事件时间均一致（表 4）。正输入、异质初态和分离到达槽三个对照分别产生 20、22 和 8 个脉冲，因此一致性并不限于静默轨迹。这是在指定测试中观测到的浮点一致性，并非将命题 1 扩展到任意浮点执行。

丢弃零幅值唤醒事件，首次在时间槽 2 改变状态与激活。将相等的兴奋性和抑制性贡献合并成净零，虽然在时间槽 2 保留了唤醒，却丢失了两个通道状态；状态差异从时间槽 2 开始，激活差异从时间槽 3 开始。将抑制性输入从时间槽 4 提前至时间槽 2，会在时间槽 2 改变状态，即使步进及块状态始终匹配。在这个 12 槽窗口内，三个违反条件的变体仍与参考保持相同的逐单元脉冲序列。因此，这些例子中，即使脉冲序列一致，也可能遗漏内部状态和激活差异；测试展示的是超出所述条件时可能出现的分组失效，而非每次违反条件都必然改变脉冲。

4.2 匹配统计量不能确定固定块轨迹

全部主对照精确保留指定的逐节点度数及权重多重集，保留原图有向邻接对的比例为 21.4%–23.7%。虽然 97.7%–98.4% 的边表行更换了目标，但这一行级指标并不等于被移除的原始邻接对比例。表 5 报告同质主对照结果，图 5 展示两种网络的全部重连点。

[[TABLE:5]]

[[FIG:5]]

同质全局短时输入下，全网 L1 中位数为 7.21%，固定身份分块 L1 中位数为 28.99%。全程平均率变化中位数为 +2.79%，停止输入后的 22 ms 窗口却为 +19.33%。因此，汇总量变化相对较小时，固定块和时间上的活动重新分配仍可明显。局部短时输入的分块差异更大（中位数 88.69%），但输入总量也不同。这些结果依赖于受测图和协议，不证明空间局部化单独导致更高敏感性。

命题 2 说明保留统计量对共同源向量施加了哪些约束，命题 3 说明这些统计量为何不能保证普遍重建输入。两者均不预测具体 L1 数值，也不使脉冲分化成为必然。实测闭环差异提供另一层经验依据。异质辅助对照中，持续、全局和局部输入的全网/分块 L1 中位数依次为 11.07%/75.31%、7.44%/32.54%、18.33%/98.52%；逐投射类别的目标强度归一化 L1 变化最大为 16.53%。这些是辅助敏感性结果，不能视为完全强度匹配的纯结构比较。

4.3 大规模重连误差高于局部灵敏度对照

对三种输入中的每一种，全部大规模重连对照的1 ms具名块误差均高于全部单次交换对照（表8，图9）。持续、全局短时和局部短时输入下，大规模重连的最小误差依次为45.55%、23.14%和73.64%，单次交换的对应最大值为39.15%、9.83%和22.70%。这一比较区分了这些对照下观察到的误差尺度。它不建立误差与改边数量之间的因果规律，因为干预影响的源、路径和端点配置也不相同。

[[TABLE:8]]

[[FIG:9]]

单次交换并非都不影响脉冲。分别考察每种输入时，19个对照中均有7个保持全部逐槽块脉冲计数，但这些图的身份随输入不同。1 ms分箱误差为零的数量分别为10、7和8。额外的分箱零误差案例包含2–8个块—槽单元格的计数不一致。因此，分箱后的零分数可能掩盖时序变化。在57个交换—输入案例中，有4个在观测窗口内保持共同原图源活动所产生的输入不变，且全部10个记录字段均逐位复现。另有17个案例虽然共同源输入差异非零，脉冲仍保持一致。输入映射诊断解释了部分无脉冲变化的交换，但不能决定非线性脉冲轨迹是否分歧（图S6）。

全部171个初始电压条件均保持逐槽块脉冲计数。早期连续状态有所不同，但末槽时全部125块的10个记录字段均与原图一致。这一结果与内核在相同事件之间的收缩、共同脉冲重置及浮点状态重新一致相容，不能作为对其他时刻或其他状态变量扰动普遍稳健的证据。尤其是，附录I.4单独施加的在线脉冲扰动可以改变脉冲序列；初始电压对照不与该结果矛盾。

群体聚合消去了大规模重连具名块差异的相当部分：按每个比较计算的抵消比例，在三种输入下的中位数依次为83.30%、75.93%和82.53%。这些数值是各自比值的中位数，不是群体与分块误差中位数之比。图S5展示全部有定义的比值，图S7随时间分别展示累积计数误差与状态误差。所测试的微小初值变化和单次合法交换均未达到大规模对照的1 ms误差范围。这标定了观察到的量级，不据此确定单位改边量的误差规律。

4.4 固定交换的脉冲影响随输入切换

在19张固定交换图中，2张在三种输入下都保持全部逐槽块脉冲计数，7张在三种输入下都存在差异，10张则随输入协议改变，在一致与不同之间切换（图10）。每一行中的结构干预固定：端点、权重和改边数量均相同。该配对比较展示了结构变化在受测脉冲中的输入条件性。但它不单独识别空间局部性的影响，因为协议的总驱动和时间过程也不同。

57个交换／输入案例分为四类。4个在到达窗口内的共同参考源输入差异为零，并逐位复现全部10个记录字段；17个输入差异非零，但保持所有逐槽脉冲计数；4个改变逐槽脉冲，却保持全部1 ms分箱计数；其余32个改变1 ms计数。这些是测得的结果类别，不是每条轨迹必然经历的因果阶段（表9）。

[[TABLE:9]]

[[FIG:10]]

种子93006的同一张交换图展示了跨输入的三个层次：持续输入下，共同源输入诊断为零且所记录状态一致；全局短时输入下，输入诊断非零但脉冲一致；局部短时输入下，1,268个块／时间槽计数单元出现差异。因此，配对输入比较不只是误差量级变化：同一图修改在受测协议下可以在输入上不可见、输入可见而脉冲不可见，或在脉冲上可见。

推论1在完整精确算术假设成立时，为轨迹不变提供充分解释；源对活动恒等式明确了活动的作用。经验诊断使用观测到的浮点源序列，且仅计入窗口内到达。记录状态是否一致另行检查。反过来，17个输入已变但脉冲未变的案例说明，非零输入映射差异不足以预测脉冲分歧。

逐槽匹配全局与焦点外部驱动后，原爆发时序仍有9/19个可见性切换，共同重排时序下为6/19。逐节点幅值多重集不变的时间重排使全局输入4/19、匹配焦点输入1/19发生切换。匹配焦点比较中，18/19个交换的二元可见性标签保持不变。一个反例足以否定幅值多重集对结果的完全决定，但不能说明切换普遍；标签不变也不表示轨迹不变。在相同焦点支持上增大幅度则有3/19切换（表19；图15 A）。各比较使用同一固定交换及其各自输入下的原图参考。因此，可见性切换不要求总驱动存在差异，逐节点幅值多重集也不能完全决定结果。这些控制不量化总驱动对原比较贡献了多少。输出活动并未匹配：G_B、F_H、G_T、F_HT的原图总脉冲数为362,200、280,500、336,900和372,400。

LIF 配对验证含 600 条正式 300 ms 网络轨迹：三张复用图、两种神经元参数变体、五种输入与 20 种图条件。异质模型 30 ms 的 G_B/F_H 切换在 seeds100/201/301 上分别为 7/19、8/19、9/19。到 300 ms，125 个块中有 116–125 个包含不同单元脉冲列，500 单元中有 401–500 个发放，平均率为 21.59–40.36 Hz，后 100 ms 仍有 1069–1934 个脉冲。因此短窗反例在真实块内失同步后仍存在，也不是沉默尾段产生的现象。焦点时间重排依然有条件性：seed201 在 30 ms 已为 0/19 切换。

以下认证先报告旧数值核的交换单点案例，再报告独立定义的固定支持权重族；二者不具有相同的结构约束。

单点审计认证了此前17个输入改变但脉冲相同案例中的16个，以及全部4个输入相同对照；36个脉冲不同案例均未获认证。剩余目标案例swap93005的Focal输入在槽4唤醒目标24，而参考在槽7才执行。其脉冲相同并不满足更强的执行分支契约。16个认证目标案例有14个在受影响目标上发放，但连续电位差最大仍可达约662.84个未校准单位。这是脉冲与分支保持，不是状态接近。

J.2 算术与仿射表示

固定执行使用最近偶数舍入的binary32运算、有限值、渐进下溢及不重排的源顺序。记u = 2^−24、η = 2^−149；无溢出时，以u|z| + η包住每个精确结果为z的基本运算误差[27]。对m次顺序加法且m u < 1，检查器使用γ = m u/(1 − m u)，以γ乘操作数绝对值和再加mη/(1 − m u)界定累加误差。单点实现用精确有理数比较验证向外投影到binary32；优化路径以binary64包络计算，必要时回退到该oracle。衰减因子使用实际舍入值binary32(1 − h)，h = binary32(0.1)。

对电压，精确仿射表达式(1 − h)V + h(E − I)保留收缩性，但误差预算遵循原运算顺序：E − I、加−V、乘h、最后加V。若相应舍入界为r_1至r_4，则附加电压误差为h(r_1 + r_2) + r_3 + r_4。不应期仍累计输入，但保持电压且不衰减电导；跳过状态冻结。共同发放将电压及其不确定性复位为精确−65，保留电导不确定性。归档THEORY.txt给出区间公式及全部调度判定。

参数族将每个标量状态表示为c + Σ p_j α_j + ε，其中|α_j| ≤ 1、|ε| ≤ r；标量盒包络为c ± (Σ|p_j| + r)。严格角点方案枚举同一仿射极值，再加同一统一残差半径，包括计算系数的不确定性，因此是同保证基线；普通角点仿真不是。入口权重舍入为binary32，发放事件乘100后再次舍入；两次误差、顺序累加及原电压和衰减舍入均计入包络。保留系数是经过验证的量，而不是未经验证的精确导数。完整公式、假设及精确Fraction oracle代码见THEORY-AND-METHODS.txt及oracle.py。

联合评分并非处处最佳。异质 F_H、300 ms 下，三个种子的联合/仅滤波/仅裕度/平均/打乱一致率分别为 0.775/0.740/0.581/0.740/0.676、0.826/0.768/0.562/0.774/0.748、0.753/0.690/0.560/0.753/0.759。保证分离比区间 [1,1.25)、[1.25,2)、[2,∞) 包含 136/321/417 个可分辨对，微平均一致率为 0.676/0.729/0.863。这些微汇总不替代目标对宏平均终点，小保证比仅弱约束真实分离。300 ms 冻结 G_B 选向对随机在九个图与目标组中有四胜、三负、两未分辨；对平均为四胜、一负、三同方向平局、一未分辨，不能推出统一迁移失败或统一优势。

N.2 覆盖与零下界

全部 4308 个正区间在 −L、0、+L 处至少包含三个不同的实际权重与事件向量及三条不同连续状态路径。十二个零下界均位于 seed301、异质 F_H、目标对 18、300 ms，括号为 [0,2⁻²⁰]，具有实际上界失效且零证书通过，搜索按预定绝对容差停止。该组最小参考裕度约 2.03×10⁻¹⁰ V，低于评分下限；这些观察不证明正安全区域为空。4320 个条件中 3477 个按宽度容差停止，832 个达到 25% 认证上限，十一个达到细化限次，没有证明间隙或零守卫失败停止；十二个零下界计入容差类。

N.3 独立实现核查

LIF 每张复用图选择目标对索引 0、9、18，每对 16 个方向，结合五输入、两种参数变体和三个前缀，共 4320 个条件。三十条原图 300 ms Atlas 参考均对全部 500 单元进行独立回放，135000000 个记录电压与电流状态字及全部脉冲逐位一致。九十次重复与短前缀运行和长轨迹前缀一致，另保留一条早期部分技术重复。认证下界的 −L、0、+L 回放与包络检查覆盖 445824000 个端点状态值。各图、变体、输入和时域固定首目标对、方向 0 的审计，使用精确有理数检查 688770 次舍入操作及 261360 个精确仿射包含关系；九十个固定评分案例另用事件流脉冲、闭式卷积和仿射导数独立核查。

完整 Atlas 检查包含固定首目标对、方向 0 案例的 60 个安全端点和 29 个可用失效见证，均与局部回放的相等性及首次差异时刻一致。C 实现在 Apple arm64 Darwin 上以 clang -O3 -std=c11 -fno-fast-math -ffp-contract=off 编译，Atlas 版本及运行器二进制哈希已归档。旧源码复现明确使用 rustc1.98.1、edition2024 和优化级别 3，早期 1.86.0 构建日志作为溯源保留。这些检查建立指定契约下的实现一致性，不是独立生理验证或硬件加速证据。

按预定规则选择的六十个安全端点与二十九个可用失效见证，其脉冲相等性及首次差异时刻均与完整 Atlas 网络核查一致。这是选定实现检查，不是对事后收缩计数进行 710 次独立完整网络测试。归档 24464 个括号可分辨评分比较另行重算；精确有理数检查针对指定算术案例，不构成全部编译器或库操作的机器验证。

N.4 事后见证与次序计算

匹配图、变体、输入、目标与方向，保留全部 30→100、30→300、100→300 ms 比较，包括未构成见证的案例。异质与同质 30→300 ms 满足 U_long<L_short 的计数分别为 710/720、630/720。异质 300 ms 时，seed100/201/301 分别贡献 120/244、154/327、120/258 个改变次序/共同可分辨的 G_B/F_H 方向对，合计 394/829，候选为九个目标组的 1080 对。不填补未分辨对；接近一半的比例仅作描述，不是与随机排序等价的检验。
